rv.q: Absent high drama, the director, Moritz von Stuelpnagel massages the play’s turning points effectively...Mr. DeVito, a master of sharp jabs of sarcasm...buoys the play with his tangy ripostes, as when he feigns surrender...but in surprising ways Sam’s travails remind us that at least they can keep sadness and emptiness briefly at bay.
Overall, this piece doesn’t land at the top of Rebeck’s impressively diverse oeuvre, and I’d wager you’ll see some things coming far faster than any fire department.

Yet despite his likability, the only parts of “I Need That” that feel authentic are those, near the end, in which the nonissue of Sam’s hoarding is momentarily swept offstage to make space for a few minutes of real father-daughter drama.
The most interesting moments of this good-natured but threadbare comedy touch on the relationship between physical objects and memory.
It just seems false to suggest such an unhealthy mental condition as somehow romantic.
It remains humorous and heartwarming at the right times, but with all the thrill of TV dinner meatloaf: low effort, over quickly and indistinguishable on the inside.
It’s nowhere near as compelling, focused or human.
But no actor can make a show work when a play is so set on phoning it in.
But it’s lesser Rebeck, a sweet-nothing of a play that’s content with the superficial.
They came for DeVito – who will hopefully appear in a more substantial play next time.
Otherwise, Theresa Rebeck’s wispy comedy about love, loss, and coping with the aftermath, is all too expected.
Fortunately, DeVito is such a skilled performer that he makes the play watchable from beginning to end despite its frequent slow spots.
Ohio is the source of all disappointment and grief in America.
But because the plot consists of a conglomeration of barely examined ideas, the whole fails to satisfy beyond the comedic stylings of Danny DeVito.
Given the play’s underdeveloped feel, it’s no wonder the cast seems to flounder.
Very little of the dialogue is of particular significance and, whether made to feel improvised or simply under-rehearsed by the cast, has a meandering quality that quickly becomes grating.
But if there’s real treasure to be dug out of the script of I Need That, neither von Stuelpnagel nor the DeVitos have shoveled deep enough to strike gold.
Its plot is paltry. Its insights are fleeting. It promises more laughs than it delivers.
The play is as muddled as Sam’s home, with characters not really speaking to each other.
After wrangling with his daughter about cleaning up his house for most of this 100-minute one-act play, Sam undergoes a conversion that is as phony as every word and action that came before it.
This is a must-see, especially for DeVito's performance.
These are throwaway bits of physical comedy, but in the hands of a master like DeVito they are hilarious moments to be treasured, hoarded and not tossed away at any cost.
Still, by the end of the play’s 90 minutes, there can be no doubt (if there ever was) that Danny DeVito is an American treasure.

If you’re a theatrical hoarder, anxious to collect as many Broadway memories as you can, you’ll need to add I Need That to your pile, if only for the chance to appreciate DeVito doing what he does best.
It's unclear if Theresa Rebeck wrote I Need That for Danny DeVito or if she reworked it once he agreed to appear in it.
The breeze that comes in doesn’t amount to much and it kind of becomes a, “My turn now,” kind of storytelling that emanates from outside the characters as written and is not organic.
This dramatization has its flaws, but it fully exposes a flawed character and forces us to face his nasty urges.
I Need That was a good concept, but theatre was the wrong method of delivering that content.

By significant contrast, Sam, the reclusive widower DeVito portrays in I Need That, doesn’t have to overcome any vile personal failings to win our sympathies; we’re with him from beginning to end, which is a testament to DeVito’s extraordinary talent and much, much less so to the play’s merit.
This play was disappointing because it was hard to connect with the characters.
